title: Acute Kidney Injury & Chronic Kidney Disease: Trends, Reversible Causes and Complication Prevention
html:
Kidney disorders change fluid balance, electrolyte and acid–base regulation, waste clearance, medication handling, and cardiovascular risk. The RN's central task is to notice a meaningful change from the client's baseline, assess the whole person, identify potentially reversible causes, prevent further injury, and recognize complications before a laboratory value becomes a crisis.

Learning goals

  • Distinguish acute kidney injury (AKI) from chronic kidney disease (CKD) using time course and evidence of chronicity.
  • Interpret urine output, creatinine, estimated GFR, urinalysis, and urine albumin in clinical context.
  • Differentiate prerenal, intrinsic kidney, and postrenal patterns without assuming one laboratory test establishes the cause.
  • Recognize hyperkalemia, pulmonary edema, severe acidosis, uremic symptoms, and obstruction as urgent risks.
  • Plan fluid, medication, nutrition, prevention, referral, and follow-up care safely.

What the kidneys do—and what fails

Healthy kidneys filter blood, regulate sodium and water, excrete potassium and acid, activate vitamin D, and support red-cell production through erythropoietin. Reduced function can therefore cause edema or dehydration, potassium abnormalities, metabolic acidosis, anemia, mineral–bone disorder, altered drug clearance, and uremic symptoms. Symptoms may be absent early; trends and risk factors matter.

AKI is a change over hours to days

AKI is identified by a rapid rise in serum creatinine or a sustained fall in urine output. Common adult criteria include a creatinine increase of at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, a rise to at least 1.5 times baseline within seven days, or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour for at least six hours. These are recognition thresholds, not a substitute for evaluating perfusion, obstruction, fluid status, medications, and the clinical course. Serum creatinine may lag behind a sudden injury, and an apparently normal value can conceal an important rise for a person with a low baseline.

Measure urine accurately and review its trend, not simply whether the client voided once. Check for collection errors, a kinked catheter, urinary retention, recent fluids or diuretics, and the documented baseline. Oliguria can precede a creatinine rise. Some AKI is nonoliguric, so urine output alone cannot exclude injury. Estimated GFR equations are less reliable when creatinine is rapidly changing; do not treat the reported eGFR as a precise real-time measure of AKI severity.

Ask “what changed?” before labeling kidney failure
A creatinine of 1.2 mg/dL may be a major increase for a client whose baseline was 0.6 mg/dL. Compare timed results, urine output, weight, blood pressure, symptoms, exposure history, and the patient's usual kidney function.

Find the mechanism: perfusion, parenchyma, or drainage

Prerenal AKI begins with reduced effective kidney perfusion: bleeding, dehydration, sepsis, heart failure, or shock are examples. A client may have low circulating volume despite visible edema. Intrinsic AKI involves kidney tissue and may follow prolonged ischemia, nephrotoxic exposure, glomerular disease, or interstitial inflammation. Postrenal AKI results from blocked urine outflow, such as urinary retention, enlarged prostate, stones, or tumor. These categories can overlap and evolve.

Assess blood pressure and perfusion, orthostatic symptoms when safe, mucous membranes, edema, lung sounds, daily weight, intake and output, bladder fullness, pain, fever, medication and contrast exposure, and infection or heart-failure signs. Urinalysis for blood, protein, and infection markers, chemistry studies, and imaging when obstruction is suspected help clarify the cause. Do not automatically give a fluid bolus to every client with oliguria: a person with pulmonary edema may be harmed by more fluid.

Protect the kidneys while treating the cause

Correct hypovolemia or shock when present, treat infection promptly, relieve obstruction, and restore perfusion according to orders. For every medication, review indication, dose, kidney clearance, and potential nephrotoxicity with the prescribing and pharmacy team. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, some antimicrobials, iodinated contrast, diuretics, and renin–angiotensin system drugs warrant context-specific review—do not independently stop a chronic protective drug or assume it always causes AKI. Avoid unnecessary exposures, maintain accurate fluid records, and communicate new deterioration during transitions of care.

Loop diuretics may be used for clinically significant fluid overload but do not directly reverse AKI. A rising urine output after a diuretic does not prove the kidneys have recovered. Reassess perfusion, oxygenation, weight, electrolytes, and renal trends after intervention.

Recognize complications that cannot wait

Hyperkalemia can cause muscle weakness and life-threatening dysrhythmias; obtain and communicate the actual potassium result, assess the ECG and rhythm when indicated, check for sample hemolysis when appropriate, and follow the emergency treatment plan promptly. Do not delay treatment of an unstable client for a repeat sample. Fluid overload may produce crackles, rising oxygen need, edema, hypertension, or pulmonary edema. Severe acidosis can worsen hemodynamic instability and respiratory demand. Uremia may cause nausea, anorexia, confusion, pericardial symptoms, or bleeding tendency. Assess the client, not just the laboratory panel.

Kidney replacement therapy may be needed for severe, medically unresponsive problems such as life-threatening electrolyte or acid–base disturbance, pulmonary edema or other fluid overload, or uremic complications. The decision is based on the whole clinical picture rather than a single creatinine or blood urea nitrogen cutoff. Coordinate urgent nephrology assessment and prepare for prescribed treatment; a later lesson covers dialysis techniques in detail.

CKD requires chronicity and a cause

CKD means an abnormality of kidney structure or function present for more than three months with health implications. A persistently low estimated GFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m², persistent urine albumin or other markers of kidney damage can establish CKD; one isolated result does not. Evaluate the cause, GFR category, and albuminuria category together. The spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) detects damage that can be present even when eGFR remains relatively preserved. A UACR above 30 mg/g may be abnormal and often needs confirmation in context.

Diabetes and hypertension are major causes, but do not assume every client with diabetes has diabetic kidney disease. Review past results, urinalysis, medications, imaging, family history, cardiovascular disease, and possible glomerular findings. A sudden creatinine rise in a client with CKD is AKI on CKD until evaluated; do not dismiss it as the chronic baseline. CKD increases risk of cardiovascular events, anemia, bone and mineral problems, hyperkalemia, acidosis, and progression to kidney failure.

Slow progression and support self-management

Individualized care may include blood-pressure and diabetes management, smoking cessation, avoidance of nephrotoxins, medication reconciliation, risk-based kidney-protective drugs, and follow-up of eGFR and UACR. ACE inhibitors or ARBs and sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors may benefit selected clients, but indications, contraindications, potassium, volume status, and kidney-function monitoring must be checked. Nutrition advice should match stage, potassium and phosphate results, appetite, dialysis status, and a renal dietitian's plan; blanket restrictions can harm nutrition.

Teach clients to know their baseline kidney results, keep follow-up tests, report reduced urine output or rapid weight gain, avoid over-the-counter NSAIDs unless the care team confirms safety, and ask before starting supplements or contrast studies. Explain which symptoms require prompt contact: worsening edema or dyspnea, persistent vomiting, marked weakness, palpitations, confusion, inability to void, or fever with urinary symptoms. A person recovering from AKI needs follow-up because apparent discharge stability does not guarantee full recovery.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Compare baseline and current creatinine, timed urine output, weight, blood pressure, perfusion, lung sounds, edema, medications, urinalysis, potassium, bicarbonate, and chronic eGFR and UACR results.
  2. Analyze cues: Distinguish acute from chronic change; consider reduced perfusion, kidney tissue injury, obstruction, or AKI superimposed on CKD; verify measurements and conflicting findings.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Unstable hyperkalemia, pulmonary edema, shock, severe acidosis, obstructed infected kidney, or uremic complications require immediate escalation.
  4. Generate solutions: Protect airway and circulation, assess volume and obstruction, seek ordered diagnostics, review medications, treat the cause, and involve nephrology for severe or persistent dysfunction.
  5. Take action: Report precise trends, follow emergency and fluid orders, avoid unapproved nephrotoxic exposures, monitor ECG when indicated, and prepare for kidney replacement therapy if prescribed.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Reassess urine output, breathing, weight, perfusion, potassium and acid–base status, creatinine trajectory, symptoms, medication safety, and follow-up arrangements.

Clinical example

A client admitted with pneumonia had a baseline creatinine of 0.8 mg/dL. It is now 1.4 mg/dL, urine output has fallen for eight hours, and potassium is rising. The RN verifies the urine measurement and catheter patency, assesses perfusion and lung sounds, checks recent medications and fluids, reviews ECG monitoring needs, and promptly communicates the timed changes. The team evaluates sepsis-related hypoperfusion, medication effects, and obstruction while avoiding an automatic fluid bolus if congestion is present. Improvement is judged by the client's perfusion and breathing as well as urine output and laboratory trends.

Original educational synthesis. AKI and CKD assessment, fluid and electrolyte treatment, medication adjustment, imaging, nephrology referral, and kidney replacement therapy require current client data, authorized orders, local protocols, and qualified supervision. This lesson is not medical advice, clinical decision support, certification, continuing education, or an official NICE, KDIGO, or NIDDK product.
